# Dewey

A Rust GUI framework whose applications describe themselves. Every widget
publishes a schema, a semantic role, and the actions it accepts, so an agent
discovers and drives a running interface over a JSON Lines protocol — no
screen-scraping, no pixel matching, no reading the application's source.

## Start here

- `HANDOFF.md` — the current state: what is fixed, what is knowingly not,
  and the one open question
- `README.md` — what it is, the widget table, and the measured numbers
- `docs/agent-prompt.md` — paste this into an agent's system prompt
- `docs/agent-protocol.md` — the full protocol reference
- `examples/quickstart.rs` — the smallest complete application

## Driving a running application

Spawn the application and speak JSON Lines on its stdin and stdout. One
document per line, one reply per request.

```
{"id": "1", "request": {"type": "get_tree"}}
{"id": "2", "request": {"type": "execute_action", "agent_id": "inc", "action": "click"}}
```

`Program::with_agent()` serves this while the window is open, so a person and
an agent can use the same application at once. `HeadlessDriver`, `RpcTransport`
and the MCP server run it without a window.

Fifteen request types: `ping`, `negotiate`, `query_ontology`, `get_schema`,
`get_tree`, `get_state`, `execute_action`, `batch_actions`, `inject_event`,
`subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `screenshot`, `validate`, `get_performance`,
`quit`.

Four worth knowing before you start:

- `get_tree` takes `since`, the `version` from your last reply, and answers
  `unchanged` without rendering anything. A re-poll costs about a hundredth of
  a full read, and re-polling is the commonest thing an agent does.
- `get_tree` takes a `viewport`. Without one the tree describes every widget
  including those scrolled out of sight; at 1000 rows that is 311 kB against
  9.0 kB clipped.
- `validate` reports what a screenshot cannot: widgets that rendered with no
  id and so cannot be clicked at all, duplicate ids, zero-size bounds,
  offscreen bounds, and text painted at a contrast nobody can read.
- `get_performance` reports what the running interface costs per frame:
  render time, `Model::update` time, the widget count, and frames per second
  where the host runs a display loop. Reading the source cannot answer that
  at any price.

## Writing an application

A whole one. Every widget follows this shape: a builder, an id, and a change to
apply when it is used.

```rust
use dewey::prelude::*;

struct App {
    count: i32,
}

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Msg {
    Increment,
    Decrement,
}

impl Model for App {
    type Msg = Msg;

    fn update(&mut self, msg: Msg) -> Command<Msg> {
        match msg {
            Msg::Increment => self.count += 1,
            Msg::Decrement => self.count -= 1,
        }
        Command::None
    }

    fn view(&self, frame: &mut Frame<'_>) {
        let rows = frame.area.rows_of(&[40.0, 40.0, 40.0]);
        Label::new(format!("Count: {}", self.count))
            .agent_id("count")
            .render(rows[0], frame);
        // `action` names the widget and gives it the message to send, so a
        // person clicking it and an agent calling `execute_action("inc",
        // "click")` take the same path.
        Button::new("+")
            .action("inc", Msg::Increment)
            .render(rows[1], frame);
        Button::new("-")
            .action("dec", Msg::Decrement)
            .render(rows[2], frame);
    }
}

fn main() -> std::result::Result<(), eframe::Error> {
    Program::new(App { count: 0 }).run()
}
```

Three things that are easy to get wrong:

- **Give every interactive widget an `agent_id`.** One without an id renders,
  looks right, and cannot be clicked or named by anything.
- `.action(id, msg)` sends a message through `update`. `.on(id, |m| ...)` mutates
  the model directly and is the shorter form when there is no message to name.
- A widget with more than one action wires them all or none: `validate --strict`
  reports one that advertises an action nothing is bound to.

Run `cargo run --example <name> -- --dewey-validate` on anything you build: it
renders one frame with no window and reports widgets that cannot be operated.

More: `examples/counter.rs` is the above with keyboard handling,
`examples/showcase.rs` uses every widget, and `docs/agent-protocol.md` is the
protocol reference. `cargo run --release --example mcp_server` serves the widget
catalogue over MCP for `query_ontology` and `get_schema`, which is the same
information as the examples in a form a tool call can filter.

## Facts

- crate `deweygui`, imported as `dewey`
- Rust 2024, MSRV 1.85
- AGPL-3.0-or-later
- 30 widget modules; 29 register a schema (`VirtualList` renders through
  `List`)
- backends: egui/wgpu (default), agpu (Vulkan-first, opt-in), web/wasm,
  software rasterizer, test recorder, null
- `HeadlessDriver` needs no GPU and no display

## Measured

Numbers and their methodology are in `README.md`; the benchmarks that produce
them are in `benches/`, and each asserts something about its result before it
prints one.

- discover → act → verify → validate, headless: 12.6 µs
- polling an unchanged screen: 100 ns
- a full `get_tree` observation: about 2000 tokens; one widget's state: 120;
  an unchanged poll: 29
- `benches/scaffold/src/bin/observation_cost.rs` prices asking the application
  against reading its source, and reports where reading wins
